title: The scan before sleep
hook: many people find a slow scan helps them drift off

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jaw, the shoulders and the belly, where the day gets stored. Your line was let the shoulders down. How many times did they come down? Day one hundred thirty-four.

It's midnight. The lights are off. Your body is tired, but your head is running a meeting: tomorrow's list, the thing you said at lunch, a song you can't shake. You roll over. You check the time, which makes it worse. You tell yourself firmly to go to sleep, which makes it much worse. Sound familiar? Here's a quieter trick, and a lot of people swear by it. Instead of arguing with your thoughts, you give your attention somewhere slow to go: a trip through your own body, from the toes up, one part at a time. Today's practice is the scan before sleep.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AND A MEETING IN YOUR HEAD.` → `GO TO SLEEP! (WORSE.)` → `THE SCAN BEFORE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Sleep has a strange rule. It's one of the few things that gets harder the more you try. Sleep researchers call it sleep effort: straining to fall asleep keeps the brain alert, the opposite of what you want. So the scan before sleep isn't a way of forcing sleep. It's a way of stepping out of the way. Two days ago, you did the body scan sitting up, awake, noticing. At night it changes a little. You lie down, and move slowly, feet, ankles, calves, knees, and at each place you add one small invitation: this part can rest now. You're not checking whether it does. You're giving it permission, then moving on. It works on two fronts. It gives the busy mind a simple, dull job, like counting sheep with more to feel. And it lets the muscles we met yesterday, the jaw, the shoulders, the belly, finally let go. Many people fall asleep before they reach their knees, and that's a success. India has a much older cousin of this. In the mid-twentieth century, Swami Satyananda Saraswati shaped a practice he called yoga nidra, yogic sleep: lying down, moving awareness around the body part by part. The name is old; in Hindu stories, Yoganidra is the divine sleep of Vishnu between the ages of the world. Different roots, same discovery. A body visited gently tends to settle. And if you're still awake at the top of your head, start again at the toes. Nothing is lost.
screen: `TRYING HARDER DOESN'T WORK.` · `THIS PART CAN REST NOW.` · `A DULL JOB FOR A BUSY MIND.` · `YOGA NIDRA, YOGIC SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVERY PART CAN REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a rehearsal for tonight. If you can, lie down; if not, lean back. Let your eyes close. Start at the feet, and say inside: my feet can rest now. Then the legs. The hips. The belly, soft. The chest, the breath slow. The hands, heavy. The shoulders, down. The jaw, loose. The eyes. Don't check whether it worked. Just give each part permission and move on. The bell holds the time.
The scan before sleep. A slow trip through the body at bedtime, giving each part permission to rest instead of forcing sleep. Today's word.
Your line: every part can rest. Tonight, lying down, scan from your toes up, and if you drift off halfway, that's the practice working. Day one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many people use a guided body scan or a yoga nidra recording in bed, lying still while attention moves slowly through the body, and many fall asleep before it ends.

myth: trying harder to fall asleep usually helps
sleep effort keeps the brain alert; the scan steps out of the way instead.
falling asleep before you finish the scan counts as a success
many people drift off before reaching their knees, and that's the point.
yoga nidra is an ancient practice unchanged for thousands of years
the name is old, but the modern practice was shaped in the twentieth century by Swami Satyananda Saraswati.

fork.setup: you've reached the top of your head, and you're still wide awake. what now?
options: check your phone for a minute.
fork.reveal: start again at the toes. nothing is lost, and the dull, slow trip is exactly what helps.

original.note: Sanskrit, yoga nidra: yogic sleep. in Hindu stories, Yoganidra is Vishnu's divine sleep; the modern practice is twentieth century.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trick to knock yourself out.
what it means: giving each part of the body permission to rest, instead of forcing sleep.
what a scholar hears: it sidesteps 'sleep effort'; its cousin yoga nidra was shaped by Swami Satyananda Saraswati, borrowing an old name for Vishnu's sleep.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya 1 (Yoganidra, the sleep of Vishnu)
sleep effort in insomnia research (e.g. Broomfield & Espie, Glasgow Sleep Effort Scale, 2005)

notes: Swami Satyananda Saraswati's book Yoga Nidra: confirm date (commonly 1976) and that he developed the method from the 1960s.
Yoganidra as the goddess/sleep of Vishnu at the end of an age (Devi Mahatmya ch. 1, Madhu and Kaitabha): confirm framing; a Hindu Keeper may prefer different wording.
'Sleep effort' as a term: confirm (Broomfield & Espie 2005, Glasgow Sleep Effort Scale).
The claim that a scan helps many drift off is framed as what people report, not a proven cure.
